Tritan vs PET vs polystyrene: which drinkware material should you specify?

The four materials in our catalogue behave differently under dishwashing, sunlight and freight. Here is how to choose between them without over-buying.

The short answer

Specify Tritan when the glass has to survive a commercial dishwasher and be reused for years — hotel pool bars, resorts, venues with a glass ban. Specify PET when the priority is the lowest possible unit cost and freight weight for an event or a single season. Specify polystyrene (PS) when you need the clearest, most glass-like appearance at volume and you can accept hand washing for longest life. Specify polypropylene (PP) when the item has to tolerate heat and repeated washing but you do not need crystal clarity. Specify acrylic when the buyer's main complaint is that plastic feels cheap, and a heavier, more premium hand feel justifies a higher unit price.

How the materials actually differ

Clarity is the first thing a buyer notices and the last thing a specification sheet explains. PS and acrylic give the closest visual match to glass — they are what you see in a hotel lobby bar where guests assume the glassware is real. PET is clear but reads slightly softer, and it is the material most likely to dull over a season of use. Tritan and PP sit in between: both are clear at first, though Tritan holds its clarity far longer under repeated washing, which is precisely why it costs more.

Durability under impact is where Tritan separates from the pack. All the materials in this catalogue are reusable in normal service, but Tritan is the one designed for a pool deck where glasses get knocked off tables onto concrete and then washed nine times a day.

Heat tolerance decides whether a dishwasher is available to you at all. Tritan, PP and AS tolerate commercial wash temperatures on the top rack. PS and acrylic should be hand washed or top-rack rinsed; hot cycles and harsh detergents dull the polished surface. PET should not go into a hot cycle at all.

Freight weight is a real cost line

Unit weight is the specification buyers most often ignore, and it shows up in the freight invoice. A stemless PET wine glass at 20 g is roughly 40% lighter than the Tritan equivalent at 32 g. Across a 5,000-piece order that difference changes the container cube and the landed cost per guest, which is why event buyers often choose PET even when they could afford Tritan.

For heavier items — stemmed glasses and ice buckets — the carton count matters as much as the unit weight. A 12 L ice bucket packing five pieces per carton is a very different freight proposition from a 1 L bucket packing 36.

Choosing by application

A common and sensible split is Tritan for the items that are washed and reused, and PET or PS for the items that are given away or replaced each season. Mixing materials inside one silhouette family is fine — the shapes match, and the buyer only sees the profile, not the polymer code.

  • Hotel or resort pool bar, dishwashed daily: Tritan
  • Wedding or event caterer, packed and re-used across bookings: Tritan for stemware, PET for high-volume stemless
  • Single-event service where pack-down speed matters more than longevity: PET
  • Lobby bar or restaurant where the glass must read as crystal: PS or acrylic
  • Beer service at volume with heavy handling: PS with heavier base walls, PP where heat tolerance matters
  • Retail or gift where the hand feel drives the price point: acrylic

What to put in the specification

When you write a specification for a drinkware order, state the material, the capacity, the unit weight, the washing guidance and the carton count. Those five data points determine the guest experience, the replacement cycle and the freight cost. Every product in our catalogue lists all five, which means you can build a specification without asking for a sample first.

Questions on this topic

Can Tritan drinkware be washed commercially?

Yes. Tritan is intended for the top rack of a commercial dishwasher and is designed to hold its clarity across repeated commercial cycles, which is the main reason it costs more than polystyrene.

Is PET drinkware reusable?

Yes, PET drinkware is reusable, but it is intended for a limited number of cycles. It should be hand washed and is not suited to hot wash cycles.

Which material looks most like real glass?

Polystyrene and acrylic give the closest visual match to glass. Acrylic additionally has a heavier hand feel, which is why it reads as premium in a hotel or restaurant setting.

What material documentation is issued with an order?

Each SKU records its polymer type and grade on the specification table, and that table is the record the quotation is issued against. Safety data sheets and any food-contact test report for the exact grade supplied are issued with the quotation. We do not publish an additive-by-additive statement unless a report for that exact grade is on file — if your destination market needs a specific declaration, tell us which one and we will confirm what we can issue.

Which material should be chosen for repeated commercial washing?

Tritan and polypropylene are the materials intended for repeated washing, and AS holds clarity in larger bowls. PET and polystyrene are the lower-cost routes and are better suited to shorter service life or hand washing.

Tritan drinkware

Does the material change the MOQ?

Yes, potentially. MOQ follows the SKU and the mould, and the material affects the production route, so the confirmed minimum is issued for the exact SKU and material you select.

How MOQ works

Can a mixed-material order be consolidated?

Yes. Mixed-material orders are consolidated into a single shipment and a single customs entry, with the material stated per SKU for classification.
